strengths: The paper proposes a clean and appealing formulation for continuous space-time video super-resolution: a local 3D sinusoidal/Fourier field over x, y, and t whose coefficients are predicted from the input video.

The method directly addresses important limitations of prior C-STVSR work, especially explicit warping, pairwise temporal modeling, and difficulty incorporating anti-aliasing into implicit representations.

The empirical results are strong across several settings: full C-STVSR on Adobe240/GoPro/Vid4, spatial-only AVSR on REDS, temporal-only interpolation, temporal consistency, and runtime/memory comparisons.
The reported gains are large for this area, often around 1-2 dB PSNR over recent baselines, while keeping parameter count comparable and inference faster than several competitors.
The paper is generally well written, with a coherent motivation, intuitive figures, useful qualitative comparisons, and a candid limitations section.
weaknesses: The evaluation lacks key ablations needed to isolate the source of the gains. It is unclear how much improvement comes from the VFF representation versus the RVRT backbone, larger temporal context, learned shared frequencies, number of bases, PSF-aware sampling, or training recipe.

The anti-aliasing claim is under-validated. The Gaussian PSF multiplier is central to the paper, but there are no targeted experiments showing reduced aliasing under scale changes or out-of-distribution sampling, and the exact parameterization of sigma is not sufficiently explained.

The method still uses RVRT with a pretrained RAFT flow component, which complicates the claim that the system avoids optical-flow-related weaknesses. Even if VFF decoding avoids explicit warping, the encoder may still inherit motion-estimation assumptions.

Continuity across local voxel boundaries is asserted to come from the backbone, but there is no formal guarantee or empirical boundary artifact analysis. A piecewise local sinusoidal representation can plausibly introduce discontinuities unless interpolation or regularization details are specified.

Comparison fairness is not fully convincing. The paper reports strong results against prior methods, but does not clearly state whether all baselines were retrained under identical data, augmentation, training length, and compute budgets, nor whether stronger backbones for baselines would close the gap.

Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation details such as basis frequency initialization/learning constraints, exact sampler construction, sigma selection for different scales, voxel boundary handling, and the substantial training budget of 16 GH200 GPUs for 2.5M iterations.

The paper relies heavily on distortion metrics such as PSNR/SSIM. For video SR, perceptual quality and temporal artifacts are important, but perceptual metrics and broader real-world degradation tests are limited.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: continuous space-time video super-resolution with arbitrary spatial and temporal sampling.
The proposed local 3D sinusoidal representation is conceptually simple and potentially appealing, especially as an alternative to explicitly factorized spatial INR plus temporal flow formulations.
The experimental section covers several relevant settings, including full C-STVSR, spatial-only video SR, frame interpolation, temporal consistency, and runtime/memory comparisons.
Reported quantitative gains are large on standard metrics, and the qualitative examples are consistent with the claimed improvements.
weaknesses: The central technical claims are not adequately isolated. The method uses a strong RVRT-style video backbone, but there is no ablation comparing the proposed VFF head against alternative heads with the same backbone, no ablation of the learned frequency basis, no ablation of the Gaussian PSF sampler, and no comparison to a 2D-plus-time baseline under matched architecture and training. As a result, the large gains could plausibly come from the backbone, training scale, or implementation details rather than the proposed representation.

The anti-aliasing formulation appears technically under-specified and possibly incorrect. The paper states that a Gaussian PSF with variance sigma leads to a multiplicative factor exp(-||omega||^2/(8 pi^2 sigma^2)); this dependence is counterintuitive for a spatial-domain Gaussian blur, where increasing blur variance should suppress high frequencies more strongly, not less. The paper does not clarify parameterization or validate the aliasing claim experimentally.

The representation is described as a continuous video field, but in practice it is a grid of independent local Fourier expansions. The paper does not specify boundary handling, interpolation across cells, or any continuity constraints, so the claimed global continuous spatio-temporal field is not convincingly established.

The claim that the method avoids flow/warping is overstated. The implementation uses RVRT with a RAFT flow component, and the paper does not clearly separate the proposed representation from flow-guided feature extraction in the backbone.

The evaluation lacks crucial fairness controls. Baselines appear to be compared largely as published methods with different architectures, training budgets, and possibly different temporal context, while V3 is trained for 2.5M iterations on 16 GH200 chips. Parameter matching alone is not sufficient to support the causal claims.

Reproducibility is weak. Many important implementation details are missing, including exact degradation/sampling procedure, loss functions, coordinate normalization, frequency initialization/constraints, voxel boundary sampling, and whether code or pretrained models will be released. The project page field is blank in the abstract.

The empirical analysis is overly narrow for the strength of the claims. There are no statistical measures, no robustness tests for out-of-distribution scale factors beyond limited tables, no direct aliasing artifact evaluation, and limited assessment on real degradations despite the method's claimed generality.

Some presentation choices raise concerns: the paper makes very strong statements such as state of the art, guaranteed anti-aliasing, and robustness to occlusions/nonlinear motion without sufficient evidence, and the method section leaves basic details such as RGB parameterization ambiguous.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and meaningful representation for continuous space-time video super-resolution: local 3D Fourier fields over joint (x,y,t), with amplitudes/phases predicted from a video encoder. This is conceptually simple, well motivated, and directly addresses limitations of warping-based C-STVSR methods.

The method has strong empirical results. It outperforms recent C-STVSR baselines by large margins on Vid4, GoPro, and Adobe240, and also performs well in the spatial-only and temporal-only special cases.

The evaluation is broader than usual for this niche: full C-STVSR, arbitrary-scale video SR, video frame interpolation, temporal consistency, qualitative comparisons, and runtime/VRAM are all reported.

The analytic Gaussian PSF sampling is an attractive contribution. It gives the representation a principled anti-aliasing mechanism and makes arbitrary-scale sampling cleaner than latent INR or warping-based alternatives.
The method is practically compelling: the main model has comparable parameter count to recent baselines while being faster than reported competitors and achieving better reconstruction quality.
weaknesses: The paper lacks component ablations. It does not clearly isolate the contributions of the 3D Fourier field, learned shared frequencies, number of basis functions, local voxelization, analytic PSF, and the RVRT backbone. This makes it harder to know which design choices are essential.

The anti-aliasing claim is plausible but not strongly validated empirically. The paper would be stronger with experiments explicitly comparing PSF-aware sampling against point sampling or learned filtering, especially under out-of-distribution scale factors.

The model uses a strong RVRT backbone with a RAFT component and very large training resources, which somewhat weakens the claim that the gains arise primarily from the Fourier representation rather than backbone/context capacity.

Reproducibility is only moderate from the manuscript alone: implementation details are provided, but there is no clear code/model release statement, and training for 2.5M iterations on 16 GH200 GPUs is costly.

Some claims about robustness to occlusions, nonlinear motion, and long-range temporal reasoning are supported mainly by qualitative examples and aggregate metrics rather than targeted diagnostic experiments.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and elegant continuous space-time formulation for video super-resolution using local 3D sinusoidal fields, avoiding explicit flow-based warping and enabling arbitrary spatial and temporal sampling in a unified representation.

The empirical results are strong across C-STVSR, spatial-only AVSR, temporal-only interpolation, temporal consistency, and robustness appendices, with substantial PSNR/SSIM gains over VideoINR, MoTIF, and BF-STVSR on several benchmarks.

The method is conceptually interpretable and computationally attractive: inference is reported to be faster than major C-STVSR baselines while retaining comparable parameter count, and the learned basis analysis is useful.
The paper includes meaningful ablations on the number of basis functions, learned versus fixed frequencies, and training iterations, plus comparisons to AVSR and VSR methods in the appendix.
weaknesses: The anti-aliasing claim is stronger than the evidence. The Gaussian PSF mechanism is theoretically appealing, but there is no direct ablation of PSF-aware sampling versus point sampling, no aliasing-specific evaluation, and limited qualitative evidence for out-of-distribution scale behavior.

Some technical details are underspecified or slightly unclear, including how RGB channels are represented in the Fourier coefficients, how local voxel boundaries are handled, and whether the local Fourier fields are continuous across cells beyond relying on the encoder.

The evaluation raises reproducibility and fairness concerns: training uses 16 GH200 chips for 2.5M iterations, the project page appears blank in the manuscript, code/checkpoints are not described, and it is not always clear whether all baselines were retrained under comparable settings.

The method relies heavily on a strong RVRT backbone with a pretrained/finetuned RAFT flow component, so the contribution of the VFF representation versus backbone capacity and training scale is not completely isolated.

The real-world degradation setting is limited. Most experiments use bicubic spatial downsampling and temporal subsampling; the degradation appendix is useful but narrow and does not establish robustness to realistic camera pipelines, compression, blur, rolling shutter, or unknown degradations.

The paper sometimes overstates novelty and guarantees: the representation is Fourier-like but local, finite, learned, and not necessarily orthogonal or globally band-limited, so claims about principled aliasing-free reconstruction and global spatio-temporal consistency should be tempered.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: continuous space-time video super-resolution with arbitrary spatial and temporal sampling.
The proposed joint 3D sinusoidal field is conceptually simple and potentially attractive compared with decoupled spatial INR plus temporal warping pipelines.
Reported quantitative results are strong across several datasets and settings, including C-STVSR, spatial-only SR, temporal-only interpolation, temporal consistency, and robustness to corruptions.
The paper includes useful ablations on basis size, learned versus fixed frequencies, and training iterations, plus computational comparisons.
weaknesses: The central technical claims are overstated relative to the actual specification. The paper claims a unified, aliasing-free continuous representation, but the practical model is a local voxel-wise Fourier expansion with no clear treatment of continuity across voxel boundaries; this undermines both the continuous-field and anti-aliasing arguments.

The anti-aliasing argument is not sufficiently sound. Gaussian attenuation of individual sinusoidal components is valid for a global Fourier representation, but the paper does not justify that this remains correct for the learned local, piecewise representation, where boundary discontinuities can introduce additional high-frequency artifacts.

Important implementation details are missing or ambiguous, including how RGB outputs are parameterized in Eq. 2-3, how voxels are selected or blended at query points, how coordinates are normalized, how sigma is chosen for arbitrary spatial and temporal scales, and what exactly differs between V3 and V3-Large beyond backbone width.

The paper repeatedly contrasts itself with flow/warping-based methods, yet its backbone uses RVRT with a RAFT flow component. This weakens the claim that the method avoids dependence on optical flow, and the contribution of the Fourier decoder versus the strong video backbone is not isolated.

The evaluation may be unfair or at least insufficiently documented. V3 is trained for 2.5 million iterations on 16 GH200 chips, but training budgets, retraining protocols, and tuning effort for baselines are not clearly matched or described.

Baselines are incomplete for several claimed capabilities. The VFI setting does not compare against dedicated state-of-the-art frame interpolation models, and the spatial-only setting only partly addresses dedicated arbitrary-scale/video SR methods, mostly in the appendix.

The very large performance gains, especially the jump in temporal-only interpolation from 29.37 to 33.43 PSNR, require deeper diagnostic evidence. The paper does not rule out protocol mismatches, data-processing differences, stronger backbone effects, or other confounders.
Reproducibility is weak: the project page is blank in the abstract, code/checkpoints are not described as available, and the computational requirements are very high for training.
The analysis of learned basis functions is mostly qualitative and does not convincingly explain why the representation works, when it fails, or how much each claimed advantage contributes.

The writing is clear, but the paper’s claims are stronger than the demonstrated evidence, particularly around aliasing-free reconstruction, warping avoidance, and generality beyond synthetic downsampling/subsampling degradations.

strengths: The paper proposes a clean and meaningful formulation for continuous space-time video super-resolution: representing video locally as a continuous 3D Fourier field over x, y, and t, avoiding the spatial/temporal factorization and explicit warping used by prior C-STVSR methods.

The empirical results are strong across several settings. V3 substantially outperforms VideoINR, MoTIF, and BF-STVSR on Vid4, GoPro, and Adobe240, with gains often above 1 dB PSNR and especially large gains for temporal-only interpolation.

The evaluation is broad and relevant: full C-STVSR, spatial-only AVSR, temporal-only VFI, temporal consistency, runtime/VRAM, basis-size ablations, fixed-frequency ablation, training-iteration ablation, and degradation robustness are all included.

The representation has useful signal-processing structure. The Gaussian PSF sampling mechanism is conceptually attractive for arbitrary-scale reconstruction and gives the model a principled anti-aliasing path that INR-based baselines lack.

The paper is generally well written and well positioned. The motivation for avoiding optical-flow-based warping is clear, and the qualitative examples support the claim that the method better handles fine detail and temporal coherence.
weaknesses: Some important implementation details are underspecified. The paper does not fully clarify how local voxel fields are stitched or queried across cell boundaries, how RGB outputs are parameterized in Eq. 2-3, and what interpolation or boundary handling is used when sampling the local VFF grid.

The ablations do not fully isolate the claimed sources of improvement. There is no direct ablation of the PSF-aware sampler, no comparison with a similarly strong backbone using a non-Fourier decoder, and no analysis separating gains from the RVRT/RAFT encoder, temporal context, learned basis, and the Fourier-field representation itself.

The anti-aliasing claim is plausible but not convincingly demonstrated experimentally. The paper would be stronger with explicit out-of-distribution scale tests, aliasing-focused visual/frequency analyses, and PSF-on/off comparisons.

Fairness of comparisons is mostly good but not perfect. V3 uses a strong RVRT backbone and partly pretrained RAFT component, while some baselines may not have comparable encoder capacity, training compute, or tuning effort. Runtime comparisons are useful but reported on a single patch size and hardware configuration.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The training setup is expensive, code/checkpoint availability is unclear, and the project-page placeholder appears blank. This makes independent verification of the large reported gains harder.

The method remains evaluated mostly under synthetic bicubic/downsampling-style degradations. Although a degradation robustness appendix is included, real-world video restoration settings with compression, camera pipelines, blur, and noise are not deeply explored.
